## Problem

You downloaded an image — or you are about to — and "it booted" is not
evidence that it is what the project built. The release ships a trust
chain that is only as good as your willingness to run it: a checksum
sheet as the identity authority, SLSA build provenance + an SPDX SBOM
per artefact, and a GPG-signed release tag. This recipe is the deep
dive on running that whole chain by hand — including the awkward case:
an artefact above GitHub's per-file cap that arrives as split parts.

## Solution

The chain has four links. Run them in order; a failed link means the
download does not get run.

```bash
# 0. Name the tag + artefact you are working with, from the release's
#    own asset table (e.g. the first staged cut):
#      tag      = 2026.01-alpha.1
#      artefact = kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-iso-redteam-ai.iso
#    Over-cap artefacts (every qcow2, iso-full) ship CHUNKED instead of
#    attached: <name>.part-000 (each ≤1900 MiB) + SHA256SUMS-parts-<name>.

# 1. LINK 1 — per-part digests (chunked artefacts only)
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS-parts-kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-qemu-full.qcow2

# 2. Reassemble — byte-exact by construction, verify the ORDER-safety
#    claim yourself (parts are named sequentially on purpose):
cat kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-qemu-full.qcow2.part-* > \
    kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-qemu-full.qcow2

#    (tools/split-release-artefact.sh verify <artefact> <dir> drives
#     this whole chunk stage as one command)

# 3. LINK 2 — the whole-file identity check
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

# 4. LINK 3 — build provenance + SBOM, Sigstore over the repo's OIDC
#    identity
gh attestation verify kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-qemu-full.qcow2 \
    -R kailash-os/kailash-os

#    (SLSA v1.0 provenance + SPDX SBOM per artefact — KA-48)

# 5. LINK 4 — the signed tag the artefacts were built from
git clone --branch 2026.01-alpha.1 --depth 50 \
      https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os.git
git tag -v 2026.01-alpha.1
```

What success looks like:

- the per-part sheet check reports `OK` for every `.part-*` line — a
  truncated part fails loudly, before the (large) reassembly
- `cat …part-* >` reproduces the file; the whole-file `sha256sum -c`
  against `SHA256SUMS` — the release sheet, THE authority on artefact
  identity — reports OK for your artefact's line
- `gh attestation verify` PASSES and names the build provenance
  predicate — the check is digest-bound to the ORIGINAL build's
  records, so it stays valid after reassembly (the split is lossless
  packaging; `cat` reproduces the attested subject's exact bytes)
- `git tag -v` shows a good GPG signature (the release notes name the
  signing key) on the tag whose lock bump the artefacts were built at

Expected output shape (abridged, per link):

```
kailash-<…>.part-000: OK
...
<artefact>: OK                                       <- whole-file SHA256SUMS line
Verified signature by a trusted GitHub artifact attestation service. <- (shape)
Good "git" signature (GPG) for <key-id>               <- (shape)
```

## Discussion

- **Why three digests, not one:** the per-part sheet authenticates each
  chunk *in transit* (a corrupt part fails before you spend the disk),
  the whole-file line in `SHA256SUMS` is the identity statement (what
  the releaser built), and the attestation binds BOTH to the *build
  event* (which workflow built it, under which repo identity) — the
  SLSA/Sigstore layer answers a question checksums cannot: not "are
  these bytes consistent" but "did the project's pipeline produce
  them".
- **The SBOM rides the same attestation:** every published artefact
  carries an SPDX SBOM as a separate statement — a supply-chain audit
  or an AI-BOM flow starts from it; keep the verified artefact and its
  attestation together in your engagement records.
- **Chunked ≠ suspicious:** the cap (2 147 483 648 bytes per upload)
  is a GitHub endpoint limit, not a project hedge. The split tool's
  contract is byte-exact reassembly, its self-test deliberately
  crosses parts to prove reassembly ORDER, and the completeness gate
  (`images-release-completeness` in the OS repo) fails CI if a matrix
  row lacks its declared build surface — chunked publishing is how
  every artefact still lives ON the release.
- **The flake-pull alternative:** any artefact, any tag, can come from
  the Cachix-held closure instead —
  `nix build github:kailash-os/kailash-os/<tag>#<ref>` — for which the
  nix fetch and the lock substitute verification; the SAME `SHA256SUMS`
  line still pins whole-file identity after the build. The release
  notes' artefact table states each artefact's surface.
- **The tag is the frame:** every other link verifies an artefact, the
  tag verifies the *release state* — the staged ladder (`-alpha.N` →
  `-rc.N` → bare `YYYY.NN`) is visible in the tag name, and its lock
  bump PR is the release review. If you intend to rebuild instead of
  download (an equally valid path for a suspicious link), build
  from this tag, not from a moving master.
- **Where a mismatch lands:** a failing link is either transport
  corruption (re-download; the sheets re-check in seconds) or a
  genuinely wrong artefact (report it on the OS repo's tracker with
  the release tag — the troubleshooting chapter's first move is
  the same checksum you just ran).
